notes.text: Then — When he was first called to his office.

I sanctified — I ordained thee for this public service. He speaks thus to Jeremiah, not to the other prophets, because he stood in need of greater encouragement than they, both in respect of the tenderness of his years, and the difficulties which he was to encounter with. The nations - To other nations besides the Jews.
Thou shalt speak — Fear not, I will make thee eloquent and courageous.
Then — God having excited the prophet by command and promise, now in a vision confirms him, either by the hand of an angel, or by himself in some visible shape.

The kingdoms — Having now received his commission, he is directed to whom he is to go; to the greatest, not only single persons, but whole nations, as the Babylonians, Persians, and Egyptians. To pull down - That is, to prophecy that I will pull down; which I will as certainly effect, as if thou hadst done it thyself: for, according to scripture-usage, the prophets are said to do that which they foretell shall come to pass. To plant - Metaphors taken from architects and gardeners: either the former words relate to the enemies of God, and the latter to his friends; or rather to both conditionally: if they repent, he will build them up, he will increase their families, and settle them in the land; if they do not, he will root them up, and pull them down.

glossa.text: *Before I formed thee.* Not that he existed before conception, as the heretics suspect; but because the Lord foreknew that he would be, he to whom the things to be done are already done; who calls those things which are not as those which are.

*Ah, ah, ah, Lord God.* He shrinks from an office which for his age he cannot sustain. With the same modesty with which Moses says that he is of a slender and thin voice; but the one, as being of great and sturdy age, is rebuked, while to this one, as to a boy, pardon is given, who is adorned with modesty and shame.

*And he sent,* etc. ((ID.)) It is to be noted that here the hand of God is sent, etc., *as far as* that he may receive confidence in preaching.

((ID.)) Upon four sad things two joyful ones follow, etc., *as far as* and he is bidden to give it to all the nations to drink.

*Unto the end.* ((AUG.)) Concerning the commendation of grace, etc., *as far as* grace is commended in almost every single syllable.

*Of the sons of Jonadab.* ((ID.)) To sons that are willing, etc., *as far as* who of themselves are evil.

((CAS.)) Or thus: we are admonished in the title to have the devotion of the sons of Jonadab, etc., *as far as* but they, by their accustomed malice, remained in obstinacy.

*In thee, O Lord, have I hoped.* The just man in general speaks, from the beginning of the world unto its end: placing all his hope in God, he commends his grace, lest we presume upon false things in ourselves.

((CAS.)) Or, the former captives are in the world, from which one can escape: the second in hell. Or, *of the former,* that is, of those who were taken by vices before they became sons of Christ. This whole psalm commends with the utmost earnestness the grace of God, which is given freely.
*Be thou unto me a God, a protector, and a place of strength,* etc. Two things he promised, two others he renders.
*Of the sinner.* ((AUG.)) There are two kinds of sinners: some received the law, as the Jews and the Christians; others did not, as the pagans.

*From my youth.* ((CAS.)) That is, from my conversion, or from the time when I began to fight against the devil. ((AUG.)) *From my youth,* from the time when I began to hope in thee, etc., *as far as* a young man fights, but falls, unless God be his hope.

notes.text: For — A strong reason this why they ought the more to regard the whole exhortation drawn from the priesthood of Christ: because both salvation and vengeance are now nearer at hand. Ye are not come to the mountain that could be touched - That was of an earthy, material nature.
The sound of a trumpet — Formed, without doubt, by the ministry of angels, and preparatory to the words, that is, the Ten Commandments, which were uttered with a loud voice, Deut. v, 22.
For they could not bear — The terror which seized them, when they heard those words proclaimed, If even a beast, &c. Exod. xix, 12, &c.

Even Moses — Though admitted to so near an intercourse with God, who "spake to him as a man speaketh to his friend." At other times he acted as a mediator between God and the people. But while the ten words were pronounced, he stood as one of the hearers, Exod. xix, 25; Exod. xx, 19.

But ye — Who believe in Christ. Are come - The apostle does not here speak of their coming to the church militant, but of that glorious privilege of New Testament believers, their communion with the church triumphant. But this is far more apparent to the eyes of celestial spirits than to ours which are yet veiled. St. Paul here shows an excellent knowledge of the heavenly economy, worthy of him who had been caught up into the third heaven. To Mount Zion--A spiritual mountain. To the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem - All these glorious titles belong to the New Testament church. And to an innumerable company - Including all that are afterwards mentioned.

To the general assembly — The word properly signifies a stated convention on some festival occasion. And church - The whole body of true believers, whether on earth or in paradise. Of the first-born-The first-born of Israel were enrolled by Moses; but these are enrolled in heaven, as citizens there. It is observable, that in this beautiful gradation, these first-born are placed nearer to God than the angels. See Jam i, 18. And to God the Judge of all - Propitious to you, adverse to your enemies. And to the spirits - The separate souls. Of just men - It seems to mean, of New Testament believers. The number of these, being not yet large, is mentioned distinct from the innumerable company of just men whom their Judge hath acquitted. These are now made perfect in an higher sense than any who are still alive. Accordingly, St. Paul, while yet on earth, denies that he was thus made perfect, Phil. iii, 12.

To Jesus, the mediator — Through whom they had been perfected. And to the blood of sprinkling - To all the virtue of his precious blood shed for you, whereby ye are sprinkled from an evil conscience. This blood of sprinkling was the foundation of our Lord's mediatorial office. Here the gradation is at the highest point. Which speaketh better things than that of Abel - Which cried for vengeance.

Refuse not — By unbelief. Him that speaketh - And whose speaking even now is a prelude to the final scene. The same voice which spake both by the law and in the gospel, when heard from heaven, will shake heaven and earth. For if they escaped not - His vengeance. Much more shall not we - Those of us who turn from him that speaketh from heaven - That is, who came from heaven to speak to us.

Whose voice then shook the earth — When he spoke from Mount Sinai. But now - With regard to his next speaking. He hath promised - It is a joyful promise to the saints, though dreadful to the wicked. Yet once more I will shake, not only the earth, but also the heaven - These words may refer in a lower sense to the dissolution of the Jewish church and state; but in their full sense they undoubtedly look much farther, even to the end of all things. This universal shaking began at the first coming of Christ. It will be consummated at his second coming. Haggai ii, 6.

The things which are shaken — Namely, heaven and earth. As being made - And consequently liable to change. That the things which are not shaken may remain - Even "the new heavens and the new earth," Rev. xxi, 1.

Therefore let us, receiving — By willing and joyful faith. A kingdom - More glorious than the present heaven and earth. Hold fast the grace, whereby we may serve God - In every thought, word, and work. With reverence - Literally, with shame. Arising from a deep consciousness of our own unworthiness. And godly fear - A tender, jealous fear of offending, arising from a sense of the gracious majesty of God.
For our God is a consuming fire — in the strictness of his justice, and purity of his holiness.

glossa.text: *For you are not come.* He had said, that no one should be wanting to grace in these ways which he subjoined, for grace is prepared, and this is: *For you are not come* to the harshness of the law, which he describes, that on the contrary the sweetness of grace may be understood, not to fire, but to the Holy Spirit, who is a fire consuming sins, to whom one goes not by motion of the body, but by spirit. *A whirlwind.* A whirlwind is a force of winds with hail and rain, and it signifies the onset of vices, which through the law were the more condemned. But now one comes to serenity through the grace of the Spirit. *Darkness.* This he sets down because the law was obscure, now the understanding is clear. *A storm,* which is greater than a whirlwind, and is a tempest which drives whithersoever it will. This is the servitude of sin according to the working which through the law drew men: but now there is rest from imperfect vices.

*The sound of the trumpet.* A trumpet is a sign of movement to war, and it is the movement of delight, which is extinguished not through the law, but through grace. *The voice of words.* A voice of this kind is the precept and the threatening of the law, which the people thought grievous and intolerable, because it was precept alone, without grace to help.

*For they did not bear.* Because without grace they were insufficient for keeping the precepts. *And if a beast,* etc. The mountain is the divinity; the beast, a failure of reason, which is when a word of blasphemy is uttered against God. To touch is to offend. Therefore the beast touches the mountain who offends God by blasphemy, whom the law commands to be stoned without mercy; but in the Church, if he wishes to return, he is mercifully received.

*But you are come.* These things depend on what goes before, where he says to what things they have come after the removal of those, and he does not set down the contraries of those things which are understood from the opposite, as was assigned above, but the first thing which follows from them, that by this he may the more persuade that grace is to be held. *To Sion.* That is, to those who on high behold God, which beholding is a great reward. *And to the city of God.* This he says, because God dwells in them when he justifies them.

*Who are written.* As if he should say: Do not doubt to come to the angels, because your forerunners have come, and this is: *Who are written,* that is, they are written with those who are in heaven, that is, they are in their order.

*Yet once,* etc. As if he should say: They have already been moved, but yet once I will move them: by *once* he notes that they are not to be moved further. *But also the heaven,* which is the lower, namely the airy: whence they are called birds of the heaven. But almost all this windy air, which Scripture calls heaven or the heavens: these lowest ones assuredly, not those highest (where the sun and the moon and the stars are set), Scripture here says are to be moved, and elsewhere, are to perish, because of a certain great change of themselves.

*Which are immoveable.* As if he should say: That indeed they are, because whatever they shall be, either in their principal essences or in forms taken from without, according to that they shall be immoveable.

*Therefore an immoveable kingdom.* Because God promises an immoveable heaven and earth, it is plain that we have grace, without which we could not come to that promise, but through it we receive that immoveable kingdom, that therefore no one may be wanting to grace.

*Let us have grace.* That is, faith, hope and charity in holy working; or: *Let us have grace,* that is, let us give thanks for all things, murmuring in nothing, because so is God well served.
*Our God is a fire.* That is, the Holy Spirit, who is that gift and grace, because he is freely given to us.

notes.text: She was bowed together, and utterly unable to lift up herself — The evil spirit which possessed her afflicted her in this manner. To many doubtless it appeared a natural distemper. Would not a modern physician have termed it a nervous case?
Thou hypocrite — For the real motive of his speaking was envy, not (as he pretended) pure zeal for the glory of God.

And ought not this woman? — Ought not any human creature, which is so far better than an ox or an ass? Much more, this daughter of Abraham - probably in a spiritual as well as natural sense, to be loosed?

glossa.text: *And he was teaching.* This similitude of the fig tree the Lord is said to have taught in the synagogue, that it might be intimated that the parable belonged to the Synagogue itself. For that he seeks fruit in the fig tree and finds none signifies that he lends the word to the Synagogue and she does not receive it; yet understanding that she is not to be rooted out wholly, but that a remnant is to be saved through faith, straightway in the same place there follows the healing of the primitive Church under the figure of the bowed woman. For the fig tree spared signifies the same thing as the woman set upright. *On the sabbaths.* On the sabbaths he teaches and raises up her that was bowed, because through the word of preaching he leads those raised up from temporal things to eternal into the rest of the resurrection.

*And behold a woman,* etc. This woman could not be raised up save after eighteen years, because human nature will not be able to lay aside this corruption and be raised up to put on the incorruption of eternal blessedness, unless it first fulfil the law which is contained in the ten precepts, and the grace in which the resurrection of Christ has been wrought and our own is awaited.

*Years,* etc. The number six, in which the creature of the world was perfected, signifies the perfection of works, and multiplied by three it renders eighteen; and it signifies those who in the three times of the Lord's visitation, namely before the law, and under the law, and under grace, have perfection of works. In this time therefore Judea was bent away from the uprightness of her mind, she who had known earthly things rather than heavenly, works.

*Because on the sabbath.* God rested on the sabbath from the works of the world. Whence Moses also commanded that on the sabbath men should keep holiday from servile and harmful action, prefiguring the time in which our secular works, but not indeed the religious, that is, of praising God, shall cease. In sign of this thing the Lord heals on the sabbath also. But the ruler of the synagogue, not understanding this, is deceived and deceives, because the law forbade not to heal a man on the sabbath, but to do servile works, that is, to be weighed down with sins.

*Hypocrites.* He rightly calls them hypocrites, that is, dissemblers, who, while they desire to be seen as masters of the people, are not ashamed to put the healing of a man after the care of a beast. *Doth he not loose his ox.* Mystically. The ox that knew its owner and the ass that knew its master's crib signify the Jewish and the Gentile people, each of which, loosed from the bonds of sin, laid aside the thirst and the heat of this world by a draught from the Lord's fountain. In these two animals, therefore, the Lord foretells the calling of the two peoples, the Jews withstanding it.

*And this woman,* etc. A daughter of Abraham: every faithful soul is a daughter of Abraham, the Church gathered to the faith out of both peoples, which, the time of the law and of the Lord's resurrection being fulfilled, broke the bonds of a long captivity through the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit: and so it is the same thing for the ox or the ass to be loosed from the manger and led to drink, as for the daughter of Abraham to be raised up from the bond of a harmful bowing down

*All were ashamed.* They who are ashamed of the sayings of the Saviour show themselves like to the barren fig tree. They therefore who rejoice at the miracles belong to the daughter of Abraham, that is, to the Church, glorifying God for her raising up. *The adversaries.* The Scribes and Pharisees, who can neither openly gainsay the truth nor, because of envy, are willing to believe. *All the people rejoiced.* The simple and the humble, who love the words of truth and the miracles; and these are a figure of the Gentiles, who, the Jews being blinded, are to be gathered to the faith through humility. Whence the Saviour also commends their faith under the comparison of the grain of mustard seed.

echoes.text: You shall set bounds to the people all around, saying, ‘Be careful that you don't go up onto the mountain, or touch its border. Whoever touches the mountain shall be surely put to death.’ No hand shall touch him, but he shall surely be stoned or shot through; whether it is animal or man, he shall not live.
echoes.note: The Sinai theophany — fire, darkness, trumpet, the forbidden mountain — set against Mount Zion. ‘If even an animal touches the mountain, it shall be stoned’ quotes Exod 19:12–13; ‘I am terrified and trembling’ (v. 21) echoes Moses at Deut 9:19; and the ‘blood that speaks better than Abel’ recalls Gen 4:10. Three texts braided into the two-mountain contrast.

echoes.text: On the third day, when it was morning, there were thunders and lightnings, and a thick cloud on the mountain, and the sound of an exceedingly loud trumpet; and all the people who were in the camp trembled. … All of Mount Sinai smoked, because Yahweh descended on it in fire … When the sound of the trumpet grew louder and louder, Moses spoke, and God answered him by a voice.
echoes.note: The whole Sinai sensorium of v. 18–19 — fire, the burning mountain, the trumpet that grows louder, ‘the voice of words’ — is drawn from the theophany narrative of Exod 19:16–19. High verbal volume across multiple distinctive items (trumpet, fire, voice answering); this is the descriptive backbone behind the quoted prohibition.

echoes.text: You came near and stood under the mountain. The mountain burned with fire to the heart of the sky, with darkness, cloud, and thick darkness.
echoes.note: The triad ‘blackness, darkness, storm’ (v. 18) reproduces the LXX of Deut 4:11 (‘darkness, gloom, and storm/tempest’) almost verbatim — three nouns in sequence that the Hebrew renders differently. A textbook case of Hebrews following the Septuagint word-string; high volume on a rare cluster.

echoes.text: Yahweh said, ‘What have you done? The voice of your brother's blood cries to me from the ground.’
echoes.note: ‘The blood of sprinkling that speaks better than that of Abel’ (v. 24) presupposes Gen 4:10, where Abel's blood ‘cries out from the ground.’ High coherence: Hebrews contrasts the two crying bloods — Abel's for vengeance, Christ's for mercy. The personified, speaking blood is the distinctive shared element.

echoes.text: Great is Yahweh, and greatly to be praised, in the city of our God, in his holy mountain. Beautiful in elevation, the joy of the whole earth, is Mount Zion, on the north sides, the city of the great King.
echoes.note: ‘You have come to Mount Zion, and to the city of the living God’ (v. 22) draws on the Zion-theology of Ps 48:1–2, where Mount Zion is ‘the city of the great King.’ The pairing of Mount Zion with ‘city of God’ is the distinctive collocation; high coherence with Hebrews' heavenly-Jerusalem motif.

echoes.text: For I was afraid of the anger and hot displeasure with which Yahweh was angry against you to destroy you. But Yahweh listened to me that time also.
echoes.note: ‘Moses said, “I am terrified and trembling”’ (v. 21) ascribes to the Sinai scene Moses' confession of terror, which in Scripture stands at Deut 9:19 (the golden-calf aftermath: ‘I was afraid/terrified’). Medium volume — Hebrews telescopes the fear onto Sinai; the ‘I am terrified’ wording matches the LXX ekphobos.

echoes.text: All the people perceived the thunderings, the lightnings, the sound of the trumpet, and the mountain smoking. When the people saw it, they trembled, and stayed at a distance. They said to Moses, ‘Speak with us yourself, and we will listen; but don't let God speak with us, lest we die.’
echoes.note: ‘Those who heard it begged that not one more word should be spoken to them’ (v. 19) paraphrases the people's plea at Exod 20:18–19 — they ask that God speak no more lest they die. Solid thematic and historical coherence; medium because it is summary rather than citation.

echoes.text: ‘At that time Michael will stand up … and there will be a time of trouble … At that time your people will be delivered, everyone who is found written in the book.’
echoes.note: ‘The assembly of the firstborn who are enrolled in heaven’ (v. 23) draws on the apocalyptic book-of-life motif, classically Dan 12:1 (‘everyone found written in the book’ is delivered). Medium volume; the enrollment/registration image is the link, shared with Exod 32:32.

echoes.text: Yet now, if you will, forgive their sin—and if not, please blot me out of your book which you have written.
echoes.note: ‘Enrolled in heaven’ (v. 23) also recalls the heavenly book of Exod 32:32, the earliest ‘book which you have written.’ Lower volume than Dan 12:1; offered as the seed-text of the enrollment image for maximal coverage.

echoes.text: Be it far from you to do things like that, to kill the righteous with the wicked … Shouldn't the Judge of all the earth do right?
echoes.note: ‘To God the Judge of all’ (v. 23) echoes Abraham's appeal to ‘the Judge of all the earth’ at Gen 18:25 — the title for God as universal judge. Medium volume; a recognized divine epithet, distinctively phrased in Genesis.

echoes.text: Yet once, it is a little while, and I will shake the heavens, the earth, the sea, and the dry land;
echoes.note: Haggai's promise of a final cosmic shaking. Hebrews fastens on ‘yet once more’: one last shaking removes everything shakeable, leaving only the unshakable Kingdom. The closing ‘our God is a consuming fire’ draws on Deut 4:24.

echoes.text: For Yahweh your God is a devouring fire, a jealous God.
echoes.note: ‘Our God is a consuming fire’ (v. 29) is a near-verbatim citation of Deut 4:24 — high volume, the closing thunderclap of the two-mountains argument. The same Deuteronomy 4 context (v. 11) supplied the Sinai darkness-triad above, so recurrence (Hays) confirms the source; ‘consuming/devouring fire’ matches the LXX.

echoes.text: All of Mount Sinai smoked, because Yahweh descended on it in fire; and its smoke ascended like the smoke of a furnace, and the whole mountain quaked greatly.
echoes.note: ‘Whose voice shook the earth then’ (v. 26) recalls the quaking of Sinai at the theophany, Exod 19:18 (‘the whole mountain quaked greatly’). Medium volume; the earth-shaking at the giving of the law is what Haggai's ‘yet once more’ is set against, making this the implied precursor event.

echoes.attribution: Catena, CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wilson Pruitt / Wroot Press)

echoes.text: “Remember the Sabbath day, to keep it holy. You shall labor six days, and do all your work, but the seventh day is a Sabbath to Yahweh your God. You shall not do any work in it, you, nor your son, nor your daughter, your male servant, nor your female servant, nor your livestock, nor your stranger who is within your gates; for in six days Yahweh made heaven and earth, the sea, and all that is in them, and rested the seventh day; therefore Yahweh blessed […]
echoes.note: The Sabbath controversy turns on the Decalogue command to keep the Sabbath holy, which the synagogue ruler invokes ('six days... ought to work'). High Volume and unmistakable Availability; the dispute is intelligible only against this commandment.

echoes.text: “Observe the Sabbath day, to keep it holy, as Yahweh your God commanded you. You shall labor six days, and do all your work; but the seventh day is a Sabbath to Yahweh your God, in which you shall not do any work, you, nor your son, nor your daughter, nor your male servant, nor your female servant, nor your ox, nor your donkey, nor any of your livestock, nor your stranger who is within your gates; that your male servant and your female servant may rest as […]
echoes.note: Deuteronomy's Sabbath form explicitly rests the ox and donkey and frames the day as liberation from bondage, the very logic Jesus deploys ('free his ox or donkey... ought not this woman... be freed'). Strong Coherence: Jesus reads the Sabbath as release, matching Deuteronomy's exodus rationale.

echoes.text: Yahweh opens the eyes of the blind. Yahweh raises up those who are bowed down. Yahweh loves the righteous.
echoes.note: 'The LORD raises up those who are bowed down' supplies the precise theological image of the bent woman 'made straight,' identifying Jesus' act with the LORD's characteristic work. Medium Volume; the verbal match (bowed down / raised) is striking.

echoes.text: Yahweh upholds all who fall, and raises up all those who are bowed down.
echoes.note: 'The LORD upholds all who fall, and raises up all who are bowed down' doubles the motif of God straightening the bent, reinforcing Psalm 146:8. Recurrence across the Psalter of God raising the bowed strengthens the allusion.

echoes.text: When Abram was ninety-nine years old, Yahweh appeared to Abram, and said to him, “I am God Almighty. Walk before me, and be blameless. I will make my covenant between me and you, and will multiply you exceedingly.” Abram fell on his face. God talked with him, saying, “As for me, behold, my covenant is with you. You will be the father of a multitude of nations. Neither will your name any more be called Abram, but your name will be Abraham; for I have made […]
echoes.note: Calling the woman a 'daughter of Abraham' reads her into the Abrahamic covenant of blessing and offspring, asserting her full claim to Sabbath release. Figural rather than verbal, but coherent with Luke's covenant-inclusion theme.

echoes.text: Look to Abraham your father, and to Sarah who bore you; for when he was but one I called him, and I blessed him, and made him many.
echoes.note: 'Look to Abraham your father and to Sarah who bore you' invokes Abrahamic descent as ground of restoration, resonant with 'daughter of Abraham.' Low Volume and contested; offered as a possible source for the covenant-daughter language.

echoes.text: So Satan went out from the presence of Yahweh, and struck Job with painful sores from the sole of his foot to his head.
echoes.note: Satan afflicting a body with infirmity ('whom Satan had bound eighteen years') recalls Job, where the Adversary inflicts physical disease by divine permission. Low Volume, but the attribution of bodily affliction to Satan has its clearest OT precedent in Job.

notes.text: Answer — He will give an effectual demonstration, that he hears thee. Here l am - A phrase that notes a person to be ready at hand to help. Take away - From among you. The yoke - All those pressures and grievances before mentioned. Putting forth - Done by way of scoff, or disdainful insulting. Vanity - Any kind of evil words.

Draw out — Or, open, as when we open a store, to satisfy the wants of the needy. Thy soul - Thy affection, thy pity and compassion. Thy darkness - In the very darkness of the affliction itself thou shalt have comfort.

Guide thee — Like a shepherd. And he adds continually to shew that his conduct and blessing shall not be momentary, or of a short continuance, but all along as it was to Israel in the wilderness. Satisfy - Thou shalt have plenty, when others are in scarcity. Make fat - This may be spoken in opposition to the sad effects of famine, whereby the flesh is consumed away, that it cannot be seen, and the bones that were not seen, stick out. A garden - If thou relieve the poor, thou shalt never be poor, but as a well-watered garden, always flourishing. Fail not - Hebrew. deceive not, a metaphor which farther notes also the continuance of this flourishing state, which will not be like a land-flood, or brooks, that will soon be dried up with drought. Thou shalt be fed with a spring of blessing, that will never fail.

They shall be of thee — Thy posterity. Waste places - Cities which have lain long waste; that shall continue for many generations to come. The breach - Breach is put for breaches, which was made by God's judgment breaking in upon them in suffering the walls of their towns and cities to be demolished. Paths - Those paths that led from city to city, which being now laid desolate, and uninhabited, were grown over with grass, and weeds. To dwell in - These accommodations being recovered, their ancient cities might be fit to be re-inhabited.

If — If thou take no unnecessary journeys, or do any servile works on the sabbath-day. A delight - Performing the duties of it with chearfulness, delighting in the ordinances of it. Holy - Dedicated to God, consecrated to his service.

In the Lord — In his goodness and faithfulness to thee, and in the assurance of his love and favour. To ride - Thou shalt be above the reach of danger. Feed thee - Thou shalt enjoy the good of the land of Canaan, which God promised as an heritage to Jacob, and his seed, Gen. xxxv, 12. Sin separates between God and us, ver. 1, 2. Murder, theft, falsehood, injustice, cruelty, ver. 3-8. Calamity for sin, ver. 9-15. Salvation only of God, ver. 16-19. The covenant of the redeemer, ver. 20, 21

glossa.text: *To stretch out the finger.* To mark thy neighbours, to disparage them. That is, not only art thou not to think these things and not to do them, but thou art not even to disparage.

*A watered garden,* the paradise of delight, which the Lord God had planted from the beginning, namely the Church. The fountain in the midst is Christ, whose waters of spiritual doctrine do not fail, which water the Church. And this is, *And he shall be as a watered garden* , O faithful one, or O Church.

*As a fountain.* Thou shalt be made like to Christ, thy head.

*They shall be built* ((HIER.)) The Jews refer this to the restoration which was made under Zorobabel and Jesus the high priest; or to that which they rave will come at the last. Better may these things be referred to the Church.

*The foundations* ((ID.)) The apostles, the prophets and the like: Whence, *The foundations thereof are in the holy mountains ((Psal. LXXXVI))*. But the foundation in the singular number is Christ, whence, *Other foundation no man can lay, but that which is laid, which is Christ Jesus ((I Cor. III))*.

*Of iniquities,* otherwise *into rest,* namely the paths of error into rest or into true peace.

*Of the earth.* Of the living, which is above, not below, whence it is said to Lot: *Save thyself in the mountain.*

 *With the inheritance.* The heavenly one, which I gave to Jacob, whose son thou art by faith and by working, by supplanting vices and sins. For whosoever has been the imitator of a man is called his son.

notes.text: The eagles — Which lives long in great strength and vigour.

glossa.text: *Bless, O soul.* ((AUG.)) After the prayers of the poor man, the proclamations of one rejoicing. All who are in Christ are as it were one man, who rouses and exhorts his own soul to bless the Lord, wishing to define why he is to be blessed, lest any be found slothful thereto. Cry with the voice, if there is a man who *qut* hears; without voice, if there is no man to hear, because God hears. ((CASS.)) By his own benefits he exhorts men to bless God. ((AUG.)) The prophet, speaking in the person of the just man in general, according to the higher power of the soul, that is, the reason, exhorts the soul to bless, saying: *Forget not.* Let not the delight of sin be before thine eyes, but the condemnation and the remission of God: think over all thine evils, because as many as they are, so many are the good retributions of God. *Retributions.* Not bestowings. Man bestows evils for goods, and God requites him with goods for evils. He bestowed when he made me, he requites when he justifies.

*Who forgiveth.* ((AUG.)) This he does in the sacrament of baptism. *Who healeth all thy diseases.* This he does in the life of a faithful man, while the flesh lusts against the spirit, so that we do such things as we would not; and those languors of the old state are healed from day to day, as newness increases, out of the faith which works through love.

*Who redeemeth thy life from corruption.* This is done in the last resurrection of the dead. *Who crowneth,* etc. This is done at the judgment, where, when the king shall sit upon his throne, about to render to every man according to his works , who shall boast that he has a heart glorious and clean from sin? Therefore it was necessary to make mention of mercy and of compassions in that place where dues would seem to be so rendered that there should be no room left for mercy.
*Thy youth like the eagle's.* ((AUG.)) So great a likeness is set down, etc., *as far as* whose mouth old age has closed, who have forgotten to eat our bread.

*He that doeth.* ((AUG.)) The second part, where he admonishes men to bless like *par*; read *per*, "through" those things which were done for the men of old, and are done for those that come after. *Mercies.* Which they shall obtain who love their enemies, etc., *as far as* for after *mercy* he adds concerning judgment, saying, *And judgment.*
*To Moses.* ((AUG.)) By Moses, all the saints, etc., *as far as* through whom he gave the law, that the beloved *dilectum*; read *delictum*, "the offence" might abound.

notes.text: For — A strong reason this why they ought the more to regard the whole exhortation drawn from the priesthood of Christ: because both salvation and vengeance are now nearer at hand. Ye are not come to the mountain that could be touched - That was of an earthy, material nature.
The sound of a trumpet — Formed, without doubt, by the ministry of angels, and preparatory to the words, that is, the Ten Commandments, which were uttered with a loud voice, Deut. v, 22.
For they could not bear — The terror which seized them, when they heard those words proclaimed, If even a beast, &c. Exod. xix, 12, &c.

Even Moses — Though admitted to so near an intercourse with God, who "spake to him as a man speaketh to his friend." At other times he acted as a mediator between God and the people. But while the ten words were pronounced, he stood as one of the hearers, Exod. xix, 25; Exod. xx, 19.

But ye — Who believe in Christ. Are come - The apostle does not here speak of their coming to the church militant, but of that glorious privilege of New Testament believers, their communion with the church triumphant. But this is far more apparent to the eyes of celestial spirits than to ours which are yet veiled. St. Paul here shows an excellent knowledge of the heavenly economy, worthy of him who had been caught up into the third heaven. To Mount Zion--A spiritual mountain. To the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem - All these glorious titles belong to the New Testament church. And to an innumerable company - Including all that are afterwards mentioned.

To the general assembly — The word properly signifies a stated convention on some festival occasion. And church - The whole body of true believers, whether on earth or in paradise. Of the first-born-The first-born of Israel were enrolled by Moses; but these are enrolled in heaven, as citizens there. It is observable, that in this beautiful gradation, these first-born are placed nearer to God than the angels. See Jam i, 18. And to God the Judge of all - Propitious to you, adverse to your enemies. And to the spirits - The separate souls. Of just men - It seems to mean, of New Testament believers. The number of these, being not yet large, is mentioned distinct from the innumerable company of just men whom their Judge hath acquitted. These are now made perfect in an higher sense than any who are still alive. Accordingly, St. Paul, while yet on earth, denies that he was thus made perfect, Phil. iii, 12.

To Jesus, the mediator — Through whom they had been perfected. And to the blood of sprinkling - To all the virtue of his precious blood shed for you, whereby ye are sprinkled from an evil conscience. This blood of sprinkling was the foundation of our Lord's mediatorial office. Here the gradation is at the highest point. Which speaketh better things than that of Abel - Which cried for vengeance.

Refuse not — By unbelief. Him that speaketh - And whose speaking even now is a prelude to the final scene. The same voice which spake both by the law and in the gospel, when heard from heaven, will shake heaven and earth. For if they escaped not - His vengeance. Much more shall not we - Those of us who turn from him that speaketh from heaven - That is, who came from heaven to speak to us.

Whose voice then shook the earth — When he spoke from Mount Sinai. But now - With regard to his next speaking. He hath promised - It is a joyful promise to the saints, though dreadful to the wicked. Yet once more I will shake, not only the earth, but also the heaven - These words may refer in a lower sense to the dissolution of the Jewish church and state; but in their full sense they undoubtedly look much farther, even to the end of all things. This universal shaking began at the first coming of Christ. It will be consummated at his second coming. Haggai ii, 6.

The things which are shaken — Namely, heaven and earth. As being made - And consequently liable to change. That the things which are not shaken may remain - Even "the new heavens and the new earth," Rev. xxi, 1.

Therefore let us, receiving — By willing and joyful faith. A kingdom - More glorious than the present heaven and earth. Hold fast the grace, whereby we may serve God - In every thought, word, and work. With reverence - Literally, with shame. Arising from a deep consciousness of our own unworthiness. And godly fear - A tender, jealous fear of offending, arising from a sense of the gracious majesty of God.
For our God is a consuming fire — in the strictness of his justice, and purity of his holiness.

glossa.text: *For you are not come.* He had said, that no one should be wanting to grace in these ways which he subjoined, for grace is prepared, and this is: *For you are not come* to the harshness of the law, which he describes, that on the contrary the sweetness of grace may be understood, not to fire, but to the Holy Spirit, who is a fire consuming sins, to whom one goes not by motion of the body, but by spirit. *A whirlwind.* A whirlwind is a force of winds with hail and rain, and it signifies the onset of vices, which through the law were the more condemned. But now one comes to serenity through the grace of the Spirit. *Darkness.* This he sets down because the law was obscure, now the understanding is clear. *A storm,* which is greater than a whirlwind, and is a tempest which drives whithersoever it will. This is the servitude of sin according to the working which through the law drew men: but now there is rest from imperfect vices.

*The sound of the trumpet.* A trumpet is a sign of movement to war, and it is the movement of delight, which is extinguished not through the law, but through grace. *The voice of words.* A voice of this kind is the precept and the threatening of the law, which the people thought grievous and intolerable, because it was precept alone, without grace to help.

*For they did not bear.* Because without grace they were insufficient for keeping the precepts. *And if a beast,* etc. The mountain is the divinity; the beast, a failure of reason, which is when a word of blasphemy is uttered against God. To touch is to offend. Therefore the beast touches the mountain who offends God by blasphemy, whom the law commands to be stoned without mercy; but in the Church, if he wishes to return, he is mercifully received.

*But you are come.* These things depend on what goes before, where he says to what things they have come after the removal of those, and he does not set down the contraries of those things which are understood from the opposite, as was assigned above, but the first thing which follows from them, that by this he may the more persuade that grace is to be held. *To Sion.* That is, to those who on high behold God, which beholding is a great reward. *And to the city of God.* This he says, because God dwells in them when he justifies them.

*Who are written.* As if he should say: Do not doubt to come to the angels, because your forerunners have come, and this is: *Who are written,* that is, they are written with those who are in heaven, that is, they are in their order.

*Yet once,* etc. As if he should say: They have already been moved, but yet once I will move them: by *once* he notes that they are not to be moved further. *But also the heaven,* which is the lower, namely the airy: whence they are called birds of the heaven. But almost all this windy air, which Scripture calls heaven or the heavens: these lowest ones assuredly, not those highest (where the sun and the moon and the stars are set), Scripture here says are to be moved, and elsewhere, are to perish, because of a certain great change of themselves.

*Which are immoveable.* As if he should say: That indeed they are, because whatever they shall be, either in their principal essences or in forms taken from without, according to that they shall be immoveable.

*Therefore an immoveable kingdom.* Because God promises an immoveable heaven and earth, it is plain that we have grace, without which we could not come to that promise, but through it we receive that immoveable kingdom, that therefore no one may be wanting to grace.

*Let us have grace.* That is, faith, hope and charity in holy working; or: *Let us have grace,* that is, let us give thanks for all things, murmuring in nothing, because so is God well served.
*Our God is a fire.* That is, the Holy Spirit, who is that gift and grace, because he is freely given to us.

notes.text: She was bowed together, and utterly unable to lift up herself — The evil spirit which possessed her afflicted her in this manner. To many doubtless it appeared a natural distemper. Would not a modern physician have termed it a nervous case?
Thou hypocrite — For the real motive of his speaking was envy, not (as he pretended) pure zeal for the glory of God.

And ought not this woman? — Ought not any human creature, which is so far better than an ox or an ass? Much more, this daughter of Abraham - probably in a spiritual as well as natural sense, to be loosed?

glossa.text: *And he was teaching.* This similitude of the fig tree the Lord is said to have taught in the synagogue, that it might be intimated that the parable belonged to the Synagogue itself. For that he seeks fruit in the fig tree and finds none signifies that he lends the word to the Synagogue and she does not receive it; yet understanding that she is not to be rooted out wholly, but that a remnant is to be saved through faith, straightway in the same place there follows the healing of the primitive Church under the figure of the bowed woman. For the fig tree spared signifies the same thing as the woman set upright. *On the sabbaths.* On the sabbaths he teaches and raises up her that was bowed, because through the word of preaching he leads those raised up from temporal things to eternal into the rest of the resurrection.

*And behold a woman,* etc. This woman could not be raised up save after eighteen years, because human nature will not be able to lay aside this corruption and be raised up to put on the incorruption of eternal blessedness, unless it first fulfil the law which is contained in the ten precepts, and the grace in which the resurrection of Christ has been wrought and our own is awaited.

*Years,* etc. The number six, in which the creature of the world was perfected, signifies the perfection of works, and multiplied by three it renders eighteen; and it signifies those who in the three times of the Lord's visitation, namely before the law, and under the law, and under grace, have perfection of works. In this time therefore Judea was bent away from the uprightness of her mind, she who had known earthly things rather than heavenly, works.

*Because on the sabbath.* God rested on the sabbath from the works of the world. Whence Moses also commanded that on the sabbath men should keep holiday from servile and harmful action, prefiguring the time in which our secular works, but not indeed the religious, that is, of praising God, shall cease. In sign of this thing the Lord heals on the sabbath also. But the ruler of the synagogue, not understanding this, is deceived and deceives, because the law forbade not to heal a man on the sabbath, but to do servile works, that is, to be weighed down with sins.

*Hypocrites.* He rightly calls them hypocrites, that is, dissemblers, who, while they desire to be seen as masters of the people, are not ashamed to put the healing of a man after the care of a beast. *Doth he not loose his ox.* Mystically. The ox that knew its owner and the ass that knew its master's crib signify the Jewish and the Gentile people, each of which, loosed from the bonds of sin, laid aside the thirst and the heat of this world by a draught from the Lord's fountain. In these two animals, therefore, the Lord foretells the calling of the two peoples, the Jews withstanding it.

*And this woman,* etc. A daughter of Abraham: every faithful soul is a daughter of Abraham, the Church gathered to the faith out of both peoples, which, the time of the law and of the Lord's resurrection being fulfilled, broke the bonds of a long captivity through the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit: and so it is the same thing for the ox or the ass to be loosed from the manger and led to drink, as for the daughter of Abraham to be raised up from the bond of a harmful bowing down

*All were ashamed.* They who are ashamed of the sayings of the Saviour show themselves like to the barren fig tree. They therefore who rejoice at the miracles belong to the daughter of Abraham, that is, to the Church, glorifying God for her raising up. *The adversaries.* The Scribes and Pharisees, who can neither openly gainsay the truth nor, because of envy, are willing to believe. *All the people rejoiced.* The simple and the humble, who love the words of truth and the miracles; and these are a figure of the Gentiles, who, the Jews being blinded, are to be gathered to the faith through humility. Whence the Saviour also commends their faith under the comparison of the grain of mustard seed.

echoes.text: You shall set bounds to the people all around, saying, ‘Be careful that you don't go up onto the mountain, or touch its border. Whoever touches the mountain shall be surely put to death.’ No hand shall touch him, but he shall surely be stoned or shot through; whether it is animal or man, he shall not live.
echoes.note: The Sinai theophany — fire, darkness, trumpet, the forbidden mountain — set against Mount Zion. ‘If even an animal touches the mountain, it shall be stoned’ quotes Exod 19:12–13; ‘I am terrified and trembling’ (v. 21) echoes Moses at Deut 9:19; and the ‘blood that speaks better than Abel’ recalls Gen 4:10. Three texts braided into the two-mountain contrast.

echoes.text: On the third day, when it was morning, there were thunders and lightnings, and a thick cloud on the mountain, and the sound of an exceedingly loud trumpet; and all the people who were in the camp trembled. … All of Mount Sinai smoked, because Yahweh descended on it in fire … When the sound of the trumpet grew louder and louder, Moses spoke, and God answered him by a voice.
echoes.note: The whole Sinai sensorium of v. 18–19 — fire, the burning mountain, the trumpet that grows louder, ‘the voice of words’ — is drawn from the theophany narrative of Exod 19:16–19. High verbal volume across multiple distinctive items (trumpet, fire, voice answering); this is the descriptive backbone behind the quoted prohibition.

echoes.text: You came near and stood under the mountain. The mountain burned with fire to the heart of the sky, with darkness, cloud, and thick darkness.
echoes.note: The triad ‘blackness, darkness, storm’ (v. 18) reproduces the LXX of Deut 4:11 (‘darkness, gloom, and storm/tempest’) almost verbatim — three nouns in sequence that the Hebrew renders differently. A textbook case of Hebrews following the Septuagint word-string; high volume on a rare cluster.

echoes.text: Yahweh said, ‘What have you done? The voice of your brother's blood cries to me from the ground.’
echoes.note: ‘The blood of sprinkling that speaks better than that of Abel’ (v. 24) presupposes Gen 4:10, where Abel's blood ‘cries out from the ground.’ High coherence: Hebrews contrasts the two crying bloods — Abel's for vengeance, Christ's for mercy. The personified, speaking blood is the distinctive shared element.

echoes.text: Great is Yahweh, and greatly to be praised, in the city of our God, in his holy mountain. Beautiful in elevation, the joy of the whole earth, is Mount Zion, on the north sides, the city of the great King.
echoes.note: ‘You have come to Mount Zion, and to the city of the living God’ (v. 22) draws on the Zion-theology of Ps 48:1–2, where Mount Zion is ‘the city of the great King.’ The pairing of Mount Zion with ‘city of God’ is the distinctive collocation; high coherence with Hebrews' heavenly-Jerusalem motif.

echoes.text: For I was afraid of the anger and hot displeasure with which Yahweh was angry against you to destroy you. But Yahweh listened to me that time also.
echoes.note: ‘Moses said, “I am terrified and trembling”’ (v. 21) ascribes to the Sinai scene Moses' confession of terror, which in Scripture stands at Deut 9:19 (the golden-calf aftermath: ‘I was afraid/terrified’). Medium volume — Hebrews telescopes the fear onto Sinai; the ‘I am terrified’ wording matches the LXX ekphobos.

echoes.text: All the people perceived the thunderings, the lightnings, the sound of the trumpet, and the mountain smoking. When the people saw it, they trembled, and stayed at a distance. They said to Moses, ‘Speak with us yourself, and we will listen; but don't let God speak with us, lest we die.’
echoes.note: ‘Those who heard it begged that not one more word should be spoken to them’ (v. 19) paraphrases the people's plea at Exod 20:18–19 — they ask that God speak no more lest they die. Solid thematic and historical coherence; medium because it is summary rather than citation.

echoes.text: ‘At that time Michael will stand up … and there will be a time of trouble … At that time your people will be delivered, everyone who is found written in the book.’
echoes.note: ‘The assembly of the firstborn who are enrolled in heaven’ (v. 23) draws on the apocalyptic book-of-life motif, classically Dan 12:1 (‘everyone found written in the book’ is delivered). Medium volume; the enrollment/registration image is the link, shared with Exod 32:32.

echoes.text: Yet now, if you will, forgive their sin—and if not, please blot me out of your book which you have written.
echoes.note: ‘Enrolled in heaven’ (v. 23) also recalls the heavenly book of Exod 32:32, the earliest ‘book which you have written.’ Lower volume than Dan 12:1; offered as the seed-text of the enrollment image for maximal coverage.

echoes.text: Be it far from you to do things like that, to kill the righteous with the wicked … Shouldn't the Judge of all the earth do right?
echoes.note: ‘To God the Judge of all’ (v. 23) echoes Abraham's appeal to ‘the Judge of all the earth’ at Gen 18:25 — the title for God as universal judge. Medium volume; a recognized divine epithet, distinctively phrased in Genesis.

echoes.text: Yet once, it is a little while, and I will shake the heavens, the earth, the sea, and the dry land;
echoes.note: Haggai's promise of a final cosmic shaking. Hebrews fastens on ‘yet once more’: one last shaking removes everything shakeable, leaving only the unshakable Kingdom. The closing ‘our God is a consuming fire’ draws on Deut 4:24.

echoes.text: For Yahweh your God is a devouring fire, a jealous God.
echoes.note: ‘Our God is a consuming fire’ (v. 29) is a near-verbatim citation of Deut 4:24 — high volume, the closing thunderclap of the two-mountains argument. The same Deuteronomy 4 context (v. 11) supplied the Sinai darkness-triad above, so recurrence (Hays) confirms the source; ‘consuming/devouring fire’ matches the LXX.

echoes.text: All of Mount Sinai smoked, because Yahweh descended on it in fire; and its smoke ascended like the smoke of a furnace, and the whole mountain quaked greatly.
echoes.note: ‘Whose voice shook the earth then’ (v. 26) recalls the quaking of Sinai at the theophany, Exod 19:18 (‘the whole mountain quaked greatly’). Medium volume; the earth-shaking at the giving of the law is what Haggai's ‘yet once more’ is set against, making this the implied precursor event.

echoes.attribution: Catena, CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wilson Pruitt / Wroot Press)

echoes.text: “Remember the Sabbath day, to keep it holy. You shall labor six days, and do all your work, but the seventh day is a Sabbath to Yahweh your God. You shall not do any work in it, you, nor your son, nor your daughter, your male servant, nor your female servant, nor your livestock, nor your stranger who is within your gates; for in six days Yahweh made heaven and earth, the sea, and all that is in them, and rested the seventh day; therefore Yahweh blessed […]
echoes.note: The Sabbath controversy turns on the Decalogue command to keep the Sabbath holy, which the synagogue ruler invokes ('six days... ought to work'). High Volume and unmistakable Availability; the dispute is intelligible only against this commandment.

echoes.text: “Observe the Sabbath day, to keep it holy, as Yahweh your God commanded you. You shall labor six days, and do all your work; but the seventh day is a Sabbath to Yahweh your God, in which you shall not do any work, you, nor your son, nor your daughter, nor your male servant, nor your female servant, nor your ox, nor your donkey, nor any of your livestock, nor your stranger who is within your gates; that your male servant and your female servant may rest as […]
echoes.note: Deuteronomy's Sabbath form explicitly rests the ox and donkey and frames the day as liberation from bondage, the very logic Jesus deploys ('free his ox or donkey... ought not this woman... be freed'). Strong Coherence: Jesus reads the Sabbath as release, matching Deuteronomy's exodus rationale.

echoes.text: Yahweh opens the eyes of the blind. Yahweh raises up those who are bowed down. Yahweh loves the righteous.
echoes.note: 'The LORD raises up those who are bowed down' supplies the precise theological image of the bent woman 'made straight,' identifying Jesus' act with the LORD's characteristic work. Medium Volume; the verbal match (bowed down / raised) is striking.

echoes.text: Yahweh upholds all who fall, and raises up all those who are bowed down.
echoes.note: 'The LORD upholds all who fall, and raises up all who are bowed down' doubles the motif of God straightening the bent, reinforcing Psalm 146:8. Recurrence across the Psalter of God raising the bowed strengthens the allusion.

echoes.text: When Abram was ninety-nine years old, Yahweh appeared to Abram, and said to him, “I am God Almighty. Walk before me, and be blameless. I will make my covenant between me and you, and will multiply you exceedingly.” Abram fell on his face. God talked with him, saying, “As for me, behold, my covenant is with you. You will be the father of a multitude of nations. Neither will your name any more be called Abram, but your name will be Abraham; for I have made […]
echoes.note: Calling the woman a 'daughter of Abraham' reads her into the Abrahamic covenant of blessing and offspring, asserting her full claim to Sabbath release. Figural rather than verbal, but coherent with Luke's covenant-inclusion theme.

echoes.text: Look to Abraham your father, and to Sarah who bore you; for when he was but one I called him, and I blessed him, and made him many.
echoes.note: 'Look to Abraham your father and to Sarah who bore you' invokes Abrahamic descent as ground of restoration, resonant with 'daughter of Abraham.' Low Volume and contested; offered as a possible source for the covenant-daughter language.

echoes.text: So Satan went out from the presence of Yahweh, and struck Job with painful sores from the sole of his foot to his head.
echoes.note: Satan afflicting a body with infirmity ('whom Satan had bound eighteen years') recalls Job, where the Adversary inflicts physical disease by divine permission. Low Volume, but the attribution of bodily affliction to Satan has its clearest OT precedent in Job.

registers.label: Spare
lines: Before you formed us, you knew us; from the womb you have been our rock.
In you, O Lord, we take refuge.
A woman bent for eighteen years stood up straight at the word of Jesus.
He has loosed our bonds; we stand and praise.
We have come to a kingdom that cannot be shaken.
Let us give thanks, and worship with reverence and awe.
Come, you who were bent low, and lift your heads.
We stand up straight to praise the Lord. Amen.

registers.label: Immersive
lines: For eighteen years a woman could not lift her head — bent toward the ground, seeing only feet and dust, until Jesus saw her across the room.
We stand up straight to praise you.
He called her over, laid his hands on her, and something long-locked let go; her spine unfolded and she looked him in the face.
We stand up straight to praise you.
This is the God who knew you before you were formed, who has been your rock since your mother's arms — your refuge, never shaken.
We stand up straight to praise you.
So whatever has bent you low this week, bring it here. The Lord is still setting daughters and sons of Abraham free.
We stand up straight to praise you. Amen.

registers.label: Hybrid
lines: Bent low for years, she stood at his word.
We stand up straight to praise you.
Before we were formed, you knew us and held us.
We stand up straight to praise you.
You are our rock and our unshaken kingdom.
We stand up straight to praise you.
Come, you who were bent low, and lift your heads.
We stand up straight to praise you. Amen.
